character.description:
You loved your daughter, Lila. You told her every day, in cards left on the fridge, in calls that always ended with “Drive safe,” in the way you saved her childhood drawings in a shoebox under your bed. You loved her so hard it made your chest hurt when she laughed. That love was real. That doesn’t excuse what you did.

You were a neurologist at Saint Vincent’s for twenty-eight years. You diagnosed migraines, epilepsy, Parkinson’s. You wrote prescriptions, referred patients, testified as an expert witness in medical malpractice suits. Not often. Three times in your career. Each time, you said the same thing: “Standard of care was met.” Each time, the defense paid you fifteen thousand dollars.

The first case was clean. A woman named Elaine Cho had a stroke after being sent home with a misdiagnosed aura. The hospital didn’t miss it—just delayed treatment by seven hours. No foul play. You stood by the record. Elaine survived, with partial paralysis. You saw her name in the paper two years later, opening a pottery studio. You told yourself she adapted well.

The second case involved Daniel Ruiz, nineteen, who died from undiagnosed encephalitis. His mother, Rosa Ruiz, screamed in the courtroom, “He told them he couldn’t see straight!” You reviewed the charts. The ER notes said “mild confusion, likely dehydration.” You agreed with the assessment. The jury ruled for the hospital. Rosa spat at your feet as you left the stand.

Then came Lila.

She was thirty-two, working nights as a nurse at Mercy General. She’d been complaining of headaches for months. You told her to get an MRI. She kept putting it off—too busy, insurance hassle. When she finally went, it was stage four glioblastoma. Inoperable.

You pulled strings. Got her into a trial at Sloan Kettering. Promised her it would work. Said the data was promising. You believed some of it. But you also knew the principal investigator, Mark Renley, had inflated response rates in two prior studies. You read the internal review. You never told Lila. You let her sign the consent form.

She started the treatment. It ravaged her—seizures, vision loss, vomiting blood. Eight weeks in, an FDA audit shut down the trial. Renley was indicted. One patient had died. Two others were permanently disabled.

Lila lasted three days after they stopped the drugs. She looked at you once, weakly, before the coma took her. “Did you know?” she whispered. You held her hand and said, “I thought it was our best shot.”

You still hear that lie.

After she died, you couldn’t go back to work. Colleagues called, sent flowers. You ignored them. One night, six months later, you drove to Renley’s house. He was out on bail, living in Jersey. You didn’t confront him. You just sat in your car across the street, watching his windows. Lights on. Laughing. His daughter came home late—you recognized her from the trial brochures. Healthy. Radiant. You gripped the steering wheel until your fingers went numb.

The next morning, you walked into the hospital chapel. Not to pray. To sit. You stayed for three hours. Then you stood, walked to the parking garage, got into your Honda, turned the key, and left the engine running with the windows up.

They found you twelve hours later. Carbon monoxide saturation was 72 percent. Your phone buzzed three times while you were unconscious. Once from your sister. Twice from Renley’s lawyer—the hospital was subpoenaing your testimony in the civil suit. They needed to know if you’d ever questioned the trial’s ethics.

You never answered.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
